sections.b: Tacitus tells the revolt in Histories 4:12-4:37, 4:54-4:79 and 4:85-4:86, and it continues in Book 5 (5:14-5:26), where the surviving text breaks off before the end of the war. Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and Roman officer, uses the draft for Vitellius's army as his spark (4:14), wins the Roman fleet and cohorts (4:15-4:16), besieges the two legions in the Old Camp (4:21-4:23), and draws the Treveri and Lingones into an "empire of the Gauls" (4:55-4:59). Petilius Cerialis breaks the rebel army at the Treveri colony (4:71-4:78). That Cerialis brought the revolt to an end rests on Josephus and Dio (below), since Tacitus's account stops short of it.

sections.h: Josephus and Dio on the same revolt
sections.b: Josephus tells it in one paragraph without the Batavians' name: a "great multitude of the Germans" and the Gauls rose "while Vespasian was about Alexandria, and Titus was lying at the siege of Jerusalem," and Cerialis defeated them (War 7.4.2, Whiston's translation). Dio says Cerialis ended the uprisings in battles after which a river was dammed by the dead (65.3). The Bible does not touch it; the link is that it happened in the very months of Jerusalem's siege.

common: Most accounts follow Tacitus, whose Histories is the fullest ancient source.

sections.b: A Stoic senator, son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus, exiled by Nero. In AD 70 he fought Eprius Marcellus over informers and over how envoys to Vespasian were chosen (4:6-4:8), moved that the Capitol be rebuilt at public cost (4:9), and as praetor led the rite that purified the Capitol's site (4:53). Suetonius says Vespasian banished him and later ordered his death (Vespasian 15). Paul meets Stoics in Athens (Acts 17:18); Helvidius's courage in speech is the Roman version of a conscience that will not bend, though the Bible places the limit in God: "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29).

sections.h: Tribute and taxes in the Bible and in Tacitus
sections.b: Rome's taxes mark its rule in the Bible: the registration under Quirinius (Luke 2:1-3), the head tax to Caesar (Matthew 22:17-21), the double drachma (Matthew 17:24-27), and Judas the Galilean's revolt "at the time of the registration" (Acts 5:37). Josephus says Judas called paying Rome a tax cowardice before God (War 2.8.1). Paul says to pay: "If it is the tax, pay the tax" (Romans 13:7). In Tacitus, Civilis calls tribute slavery (4:17) and Cerialis answers that "there can be no peace among nations without armies, no armies without pay, and no pay without taxes" (4:74).
sections.refs: Luke 2:1-3; Matthew 22:17-21; Matthew 17:24-27; Acts 5:37; Romans 13:6-7; Histories 4:17; Histories 4:74

sections.h: The tax that moved to the Capitol
sections.b: After the war Vespasian "laid a tribute upon the Jews wheresoever they were, and enjoined every one of them to bring two drachmae every year into the Capitol, as they used to pay the same to the temple at Jerusalem" (War 7.6.6, Whiston). Dio says it was two denarii to Jupiter Capitolinus (65.7).

Tacitus says Veleda, a maiden of the Bructeri, had predicted the Germans' success and the legions' destruction, so her authority was at its height in AD 70 (4:61). A Roman legate was sent to her among the gifts (4:61). She lived in a tall tower and a relative carried questions and answers (4:65). Wikipedia says her name probably means "seeress." The Bible's prophetesses were Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4), Anna (Luke 2:36) and Philip's four daughters (Acts 21:9); none was worshiped, and Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes when crowds treated them as gods (Acts 14:14-15).
sections.refs: Histories 4:61; Histories 4:65; Judges 4:4; Luke 2:36; Acts 21:9; Acts 14:14-15

sections.b: Tacitus says Vespasian, at Alexandria, was approached by a blind man and a man with a sick hand on the advice of "the god Serapis," healed both, and then went into Serapis's temple to ask about the empire (4:81-4:82). He gives the Egyptian priests' story of how a statue of the god came from Sinope on the Black Sea to Alexandria under the first Ptolemy (4:83-4:84), and the rival views that the god was Aesculapius, Osiris, Jupiter or Pluto. Plutarch tells the same story of Ptolemy's dream and the Sinope statue (On Isis and Osiris 28).

sections.h: What the Bible says of such gods
sections.b: The Bible calls the gods of the nations empty (Psalm 115:4-8; Isaiah 44:9-10) and, in Paul's words, what is sacrificed to them goes "to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20; compare Deuteronomy 32:17). Christian readers weigh these two lines; the site's topic The Divine Council sets out the views.

sections.h: Stoics in Tacitus and in Acts
sections.b: Tacitus says Helvidius Priscus followed teachers of philosophy "who hold that nothing is good but what is honorable and nothing is bad but what is shameful" (4:5). That is one tenet of the school the site calls Stoic; Wikipedia names Helvidius and Musonius Rufus as Stoics, and Musonius appears at 4:10. In Acts "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also took" Paul on in Athens (Acts 17:18).

sections.h: Cyrene in the Bible and in Tacitus
sections.b: Cyrene was a Greek city of North Africa. Its people appear in the Bible at the cross (Mark 15:21), in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), at Pentecost (Acts 2:10) and in the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1). Tacitus tells that the people of Cyrene brought an extortion charge against a Roman, Antonius Flamma, who was exiled for cruelty (4:45). Josephus tells of unrest among its Jews after the war (War 7.11.1).
sections.refs: Mark 15:21; Acts 2:10; Acts 6:9; Acts 13:1; Histories 4:45; War 7.11.1

sections.h: Parthians in Acts and in Tacitus
sections.b: Parthia was the empire east of Rome. Parthians are in the Pentecost crowd: "We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites" (Acts 2:9). In AD 69 King Vologesus offered Vespasian forty thousand horsemen; he thanked the king and declined (Tacitus, Histories 4:51).

Domitian takes the name of Caesar and moves into the emperor's house without ruling (4:2), takes the city praetorship (4:39), speaks modestly in the Senate (4:40), is held at Lugdunum by Mucianus (4:85) and sends secret word to Cerialis (4:86). Suetonius agrees that he planned an "uncalled for" campaign against Gaul and the Germanies and feigned an interest in poetry (Domitian 2.1-2.2). Josephus says he marched and won Gaul (War 7.4.2). Many readers place Revelation in his reign (Revelation 1:9; Revelation 13:4); the date is argued.

sections.h: Command of the Guard in Book 4
sections.b: Arrius Varus commanded the Praetorian Guard after the victory (4:2); Mucianus removed him and put Arrecinus Clemens in his place (4:68). The Vitellianist soldiers were taken into the Praetorian camp and discharged by degrees (4:46). Philippians 1:13 says Paul's chains were known "by the whole praetorium and by everyone else."

Tacitus: Vespasian handed Titus the strongest part of the army "to finish what was left of the Jewish war" (4:51). Josephus: Titus marched from Alexandria by Pelusium and Gaza to Caesarea (War 4.11.5). Jesus had said: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). The temple burned on the tenth of Lous, the day it was burned by the king of Babylon (War 6.4.5).

Tacitus's Lucilius Bassus is sent to Campania in AD 70 (4:3). Josephus has a Lucilius Bassus sent as legate into Judea, who takes Herodium (War 7.6.1). Same man: likely; neither writer says so outright.

Mucianus entered Rome and "drew everything to himself at once" (4:11); had a young man he feared killed on the Appian Road (4:11); shielded the informers (4:44); and moved Antonius Primus and Arrius Varus out of power (4:39; 4:68; 4:80). Josephus shows him meeting Vespasian at Berytus as governor of Syria (War 4.10.6).

The Senate met on 1 January AD 70 (4:39), voted Vespasian an emperor's honors (4:3), debated how to choose envoys (4:6-4:8), swore an oath against informing (4:41) and tried Publius Celer for testifying against Barea Soranus (4:10; 4:40). Sources: Tacitus, Histories 4. Luke uses a different Roman courtroom: Paul's appeal is to "Caesar's judgment seat" (Acts 25:10-12).

sections.h: Army abuses and mutiny, in Tacitus and Luke
sections.b: Tacitus shows draft officials selling exemptions (4:14), a bonus demanded as an excuse for mutiny (4:19) and generals murdered by their own men (4:36). John the Baptist told soldiers: "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges. Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14).

sections.h: Proconsul, legate and procurator in Africa
sections.b: Tacitus explains how Africa's legion passed from the proconsul to a legate under Caligula (4:48) and names Baebius Massa as a procurator there (4:50). Acts has proconsuls (Acts 13:7; Acts 18:12; Acts 19:38); Josephus calls Coponius and Pilate procurators (War 2.8.1; War 2.9.2). The Festus of Acts (Acts 24:27) is Porcius Festus; Tacitus's Valerius Festus (4:49) is another man.

Vespasian waited at Alexandria for the summer sailing (4:81). There, says Tacitus, a blind man and a man with a sick hand begged him for a cure, and he went alone into Serapis's temple (4:81-4:82). Josephus says Egypt fed Rome, so Vespasian took it first (War 4.10.5), that Tiberius Alexander made the legions swear to him (War 4.10.6), and that Alexandria was "the greatest of all cities next to Rome" (War 4.11.5). Acts names Alexandrians in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), Apollos (Acts 18:24) and ships (Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11).

At 4:51-4:52 Vespasian gives Titus the strongest part of the army, and Titus begs his father to be forgiving to Domitian. Josephus adds Titus's march from Alexandria (War 4.11.5). Not Paul's Titus, who was "a Greek" and "my partner and my fellow worker" (Galatians 2:3; 2 Corinthians 8:23).

Tacitus tells that at Alexandria Vespasian healed a blind man with spit and a man with a damaged hand by treading on it, after asking doctors (4:81), and that in Serapis's temple he saw Basilides, who was days away (4:82). Suetonius (Vespasian 7) and Dio (65.8) tell it too. Josephus does not. Meier, as quoted by Dickson, reads it as a show of legitimacy; Eve as propaganda. Compare the Gospels (Mark 8:23; Mark 3:5).

Josephus says he told Vespasian after Jotapata, "Thou, O Vespasian, art Caesar and emperor, thou, and this thy son" (War 3.8.9). Suetonius (Vespasian 5.6) and Dio (65.1) report it. Tacitus does not mention Josephus here but reports the oracle of rulers from Judea at 5:13.

Josephus tells the Capitol's burning and Sabinus's death (War 4.11.4), Vespasian's time in Alexandria without the healings (War 4.11.5), the German revolt in a paragraph (War 7.4.2), the Sarmatian raid (War 7.4.3), the triumph (War 7.5.6) and the tax to the Capitol (War 7.6.6). He is the only one of the three to make Domitian a conqueror of Gaul (War 7.4.2); Whiston's footnote suggests he wrote kindly because Domitian was a patron.

Tacitus: the work was given to Lucius Vestinius; soothsayers said to keep the footprint and raise the height; the foundation rite was on 21 June, with Helvidius Priscus as praetor, Vestals, a pig, a sheep and a bull (4:53). Suetonius: Vespasian cleared the rubble himself (Vespasian 8.5). Wikipedia: dedicated AD 75. The Jews' temple tax went to the Capitol after AD 70 (War 7.6.6). The Bible's own rebuilding: Ezra 3:10-13; Haggai 2:9.

Domitian had the consulships Vitellius gave canceled and moved a censor's funeral for Flavius Sabinus (4:47). Josephus calls Domitian "his brother's son" and tells how Sabinus seized the Capitol and was killed (War 4.11.4).

Josephus: Tiberius Alexander was "then governor of Egypt and of Alexandria" when Vespasian wrote to him, and he had the legions swear fidelity (War 4.10.6). Earlier, as governor of the city, he sent soldiers against a Jewish rising and "fifty thousand of them lay dead" (War 2.18.7-8).

The low Rhine is taken as an omen that the rivers desert Rome (4:26); the Druids read the Capitol's fire as heaven's anger (4:54); soothsayers set the Capitol's footprint and warn against using gold meant for another use (4:53); Vespasian reads a name as the god's answer (4:82). The Bible's tests: Deuteronomy 18:22 and Deuteronomy 13:1-3.
Tacitus names Queen Berenice beside Agrippa as backing Vespasian (2:81); at 4:39 the allied kings are thanked. Luke has "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice" to see Festus (Acts 25:13).

Book 4 opens after Vitellius's death with soldiers hunting the losers in Rome (4:1), the Senate honoring Vespasian (4:3) and Domitian standing in for his father (4:2). Josephus compresses the same weeks into the Capitol fight and the killing of Vitellius (War 4.11.4).

sections.h: Tacitus's way of telling it in Book 4
sections.b: He gives the speeches of both sides, including Rome's enemies (4:14; 4:17; 4:64; 4:73-4:74). He marks hearsay (4:49; 4:61) and gives the Egyptian priests' version of Serapis, saying Roman writers had not yet told it (4:83). He speaks as a Roman who lived through the later troubles (4:50).

sections.h: Rome in Tacitus, Book 4, and the Bible's Rome
sections.b: The Book 4 world: a Senate that debates and fears, informers, soldiers who make emperors, grain from Africa and Egypt (4:38; 4:52), and provinces such as Syria, Illyricum and Spain. Josephus's Varus, governor of Syria in Herod's last years, is very likely the Varus whose army Germany destroyed (4:17). The Appian Road of Acts 28:15 appears at 4:11, and Pontus, Cyrene and Asia at 4:83, 4:45 and 4:10.
sections.refs: Histories 4:11; Histories 4:17; Histories 4:38; Acts 28:15; Acts 2:9; Mark 15:21

sections.b: Sabinus claims descent from "the divine Julius" (4:55). Vespasian is shown signs of heaven's favor at Alexandria (4:81). Suetonius reports his last joke, "Woe's me. Methinks I'm turning into a god" (Vespasian 23.4). In Acts the crowd shouts of Herod, "It's a god speaking, not a man!" and "an angel of the Lord struck him" (Acts 12:22-23). Caligula went so far "as to take himself to be a god" and tried to place his statues in the temple (War 2.10.1).

Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio each tell that Vespasian healed a blind man with spit and a second man with a damaged limb (Histories 4:81; Vespasian 7.2-3; Dio 65.8). Readers take it as staged (Meier, as quoted by Dickson), as propaganda (Eve), as ordinary recovery (Tacitus's doctors), or as something more. The Gospels have spit-cures (Mark 7:33; Mark 8:23; John 9:6) and a withered hand (Mark 3:1-5); the Bible tests signs by what they ask you to worship (Deuteronomy 13:1-3) and warns of lying wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

claude.title: A pair of cures
claude.body: Claude's reading: the Alexandria pair, sight and a damaged limb, is the pair Isaiah 35:5-6 and Matthew 11:5 list. It may be chance, since eyes and limbs are common ailments.

sections.h: Healing at Alexandria and in the Gospels
sections.b: Vespasian asks doctors first (4:81); the woman in the Gospels had "spent every penny she owned" on doctors (Mark 5:26) and Jesus quotes the proverb "Doctor, cure yourself!" (Luke 4:23). Aesculapius, the healer god, is one of the gods Serapis was said to be (4:84).

Egypt feeds Rome, so Vespasian takes it first (Josephus, War 4.10.5). In Alexandria he goes into Serapis's temple, and Tacitus tells the Greek-Egyptian story of how the god came (4:81-4:84). Joseph's family fled to Egypt in a dream (Matthew 2:13), and Pharaoh's wise men could not read his dream (Genesis 41:8).

sections.h: Jerusalem in the year Rome rebuilt its Capitol
sections.b: Tacitus records Rome rebuilding the Capitol in June AD 70 (4:53) and sending Titus to finish the Jewish war (4:51). Josephus puts the burning of the temple on the tenth of Lous (War 6.4.5), and Vespasian redirects the temple tax to the Capitol (War 7.6.6).

Rome had ten days' grain left until Vespasian's ships came (4:52); the camp at the Old Camp ate roots and grass (4:60). Acts has a famine "in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28). Samaria's siege famine is in 2 Kings 6:25.

Civilis binds the chiefs by "the curses they swear in their oaths" (4:15); soldiers swear and mumble Vespasian's name (4:31); the senators swear by the gods (4:41); Civilis cuts his dyed hair when his vow is done (4:61). The Law's Nazirite shaves and burns his hair at the end of his vow (Numbers 6:18), and Acts 18:18 has someone, Paul or Aquila, cutting his hair for a vow. Jesus: "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34).
sections.refs: Histories 4:15; Histories 4:41; Histories 4:61; Numbers 6:18; Acts 18:18; Matthew 5:34

sections.b: The Druids read the Capitol's fire as the end of Rome (4:54); Veleda foretold the legions' end (4:61). The Bible's test is Deuteronomy 18:22.

claude.title: Two sanctuaries on fire
claude.body: Claude's reading: in AD 69-70 the Druids read the Capitol's fire after the fact; Josephus reads the Temple's fire as an old doom (War 6.4.5), and Jesus had said not one stone would be left (Matthew 24:2).

sections.b: A king dreams that a god wants a statue and the Egyptian priests cannot read it (4:83). Pharaoh's wise men could not read his dreams either (Genesis 41:8; Genesis 41:25). Joseph in Matthew is guided by dreams in and out of Egypt (Matthew 2:13; Matthew 2:19-20).

sections.h: Two senators on obeying a bad emperor
sections.b: Marcellus: "while I pray for good emperors, I can put up with whatever kind we get" (4:8). Cerialis: bear bad rulers like bad weather (4:74). Paul: pray for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1-2), submit for conscience's sake (Romans 13:5), but "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29).

Marcellus wants the Senate's envoys to Vespasian drawn by lot (4:6; 4:8). The apostles drew lots for Matthias (Acts 1:26), and Proverbs says "every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33).

The low Rhine was taken by soldiers as a sign that even the rivers were deserting Rome (4:26). Jesus: "great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:11); Josephus: false prophets promising "miraculous signs" in Jerusalem (War 6.5.2).

Vocula prays to Jupiter Best and Greatest and Quirinus (4:58); Serapis "boards the ships" in the popular story (4:84). At Lystra Barnabas is called Zeus (Acts 14:12). The Bible: Psalm 115:4-8; Isaiah 44:9-10; 1 Corinthians 10:20.
Helvidius purified the Capitol's site with a pig, a sheep and a bull (4:53). Israel's law counts the pig unclean (Leviticus 11:7), and Isaiah lists pig's blood among rejected offerings (Isaiah 66:3).
Ptolemy's envoys are sent to the Pythian Apollo (4:83). Luke's slave girl at Philippi "had a Python spirit" (Acts 16:16).

sections.h: The oracle of rulers from Judea
sections.b: Josephus applies the old oracle that "one from their country should become governor of the habitable earth" to Vespasian (War 6.5.4), and tells Vespasian he will be emperor (War 3.8.9). Vespasian asks the god about the empire at Alexandria (Tacitus, 4:82). Tacitus's version of the oracle is at 5:13.

Marcellus says friendship with Nero was nerve-racking (4:8); Montanus charges that informers wanted a worse tyrant than Nero's slowness allowed (4:42). The New Testament does not name Nero; Paul appeals to "Caesar's judgment seat" (Acts 25:10-12).
Tacitus: Agrippa and Queen Berenice backed Vespasian (2:81), and the Senate thanked the allied kings (4:39). Luke: "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13).

After the victory slaves betrayed their rich masters (4:1); Piso's slave gave a noble lie (4:50); a slave of Vergilius Capito was hanged (4:3). Jesus warned that people "will hand each other over" (Matthew 24:10).
The Titus of Galatians, 2 Corinthians and Titus is Paul's coworker, "a Greek" (Galatians 2:3). The emperor Titus, Vespasian's son, is sent against Jerusalem in Tacitus 4:51; not the same person.

Tacitus shows the young Domitian as Caesar in AD 70 without real power (4:2; 4:39; 4:85-4:86). Suetonius agrees (Domitian 1.3; 2.1-2.2). Revelation's date, and whether Domitian's reign is its setting, is argued on this page.

Tacitus shows the Germans learning siege methods from Rome at the Old Camp (4:23); Titus used Rome's own at Jerusalem (War 5.12.1; War 6.4.1). Luke 19:43 and Luke 21:20 describe the siege in outline. Matthew 24:6 speaks of "wars and reports of wars."
